5 Kanji Apps Compared: Find Your Study Fit in 2026

Kanjidon Team · Feb 3, 2026

Do you want to read more comfortably, remember vocabulary or write kanji by hand? Those goals call for different tools. Here are five options, the differences that matter when choosing, and a short trial you can run before committing to a new routine.

This feature comparison draws on official documentation checked on September 9, 2026. Kanjidon is our app. Suggestions about who might prefer each tool are editorial judgments, not findings from a comparative learning study.

Five apps and their different approaches

AppWhat it offersConsider it whenTrade-off to assess
KanjidonCollectible cards, quizzes and reviews for kanji and vocabulary arranged by JLPT level.You want to study on your phone and collecting cards helps you return.Add reading, listening and grammar: finishing quizzes alone does not establish complete exam readiness.
WaniKaniA guided curriculum with mnemonics and reviews; meaning answers use English.You prefer a planned sequence and are comfortable studying in English.Lessons unlock through the curriculum, so consider how freely you want to choose your material.
AnkiCustomizable flashcards, multimedia content and scheduled reviews.You want to build cards from words in your own books or courses.You need to choose or create a deck and check the quality of its cards.
RingotanKanji handwriting exercises with spaced repetition on iOS and Android.You want to practise producing written forms as well as recognizing them.Try writing without tracing a model and decide whether the exercise suits your goal.
DuolingoA Japanese course with character exercises; availability depends on the course.You want an introductory language course that also introduces kanji.Check the exercises in your chosen course: features can differ by teaching language and platform.

Where I would start for each goal

  • For a deck built from your own reading, start by considering Anki. For a ready-made sequence, look at WaniKani.
  • For handwriting, try Ringotan. For quizzes and collecting cards on your phone, try Kanjidon.
  • For a general introduction to Japanese, consider Duolingo and check the kanji exercises available in your course language.

A short trial before you decide

  • Complete an introductory lesson and a review. Is it clear what you are learning and why an answer is wrong?
  • Recall a studied word without hints. Separate being able to read it from recognizing it among answer choices.
  • Try reading that word in another sentence. If handwriting matters, also write without tracing.
  • Choose one main review routine. Add another tool when it fills a different need.

Check language, devices and access

Use the official links below to check the teaching language, supported devices, included content and renewal terms for your country. For Anki, follow the official links to AnkiMobile on iOS and AnkiDroid on Android. An app with a similar name may be a different product.
